name: Grasshopper Sweep
description: Master Grasshopper Sweep in BJJ. Inverted guard sweep using hip elevation to transition from Grasshopper Guard to Mount. Success: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.
overview:
The Grasshopper Sweep is a dynamic elevation sweep executed from the inverted Grasshopper Guard position, designed to off-balance a standing or kneeling opponent and transition directly to Mount. This technique leverages the unique mechanics of inverted guards where the bottom practitioner uses their shoulders as a base while driving their hips upward into the opponent's center of mass.

The sweep capitalizes on the opponent's forward commitment or narrow base, using leg hooks behind their knees combined with explosive hip elevation to lift and dump them backward. Unlike traditional sweeps that rely on lateral off-balancing, the Grasshopper Sweep works primarily in the vertical plane, making it particularly effective when opponents attempt to pressure forward into the guard.

Strategically, this sweep functions as a high-reward option within the Grasshopper Guard system. When opponents recognize the leg entanglement threats from grasshopper and begin backing away or widening their base defensively, they often create the exact conditions needed for this sweep. The technique requires precise timing and substantial core strength to execute, but when landed correctly, it bypasses the half guard and side control positions entirely, placing you directly in mount with significant momentum advantage.
key_principles: Hip elevation must precede the sweep motion - drive hips toward ceiling before attempting to tip opponent
Leg hooks behind opponent's knees create the fulcrum point for the sweep
Opponent's forward pressure or weight commitment provides the energy for the sweep
Shoulder base must remain stable throughout - rolling onto one shoulder kills the technique
Core engagement is continuous from initiation through mount establishment
The sweep works best when opponent's base is narrow or weight is forward
Follow the opponent through the sweep rather than stopping at elevation
setup_requirements: Established Grasshopper Guard with inverted posture and elevated hips
At least one leg hook behind opponent's knee or thigh
Opponent standing or in combat base with accessible lower body
Sufficient core engagement to maintain hip elevation throughout technique
Clear path for opponent to fall backward without obstruction

execution_steps.description: From seated or open guard, invert your body placing weight on shoulder blades with hips elevated above torso level. Maintain strong core engagement to keep hips high.
execution_steps.timing: 2-3 seconds to establish stable inverted base

execution_steps.description: Thread both legs behind opponent's knees, creating hooks with your feet curling around the back of their thighs. The hooks should be deep enough to control their base.
execution_steps.timing: As opponent steps into range or commits weight forward

execution_steps.description: Establish grips on opponent's ankles, heels, or pants near the ankle area. These grips prevent them from stepping back and provide additional control for the elevation.
Drive hips explosively toward the ceiling while simultaneously pulling opponent's ankles toward you and extending your legs. Your hip elevation lifts them off the ground.
execution_steps.timing: When opponent's weight shifts forward or they attempt to pressure

execution_steps.description: As opponent tips backward, continue extending your legs and driving your hips upward. Follow their falling motion with your body, beginning to rotate from inverted to upright.
As opponent lands on their back, complete your rotation and land in mount position. Immediately establish base with hands posted and hips heavy on their torso.
execution_steps.timing: 0.5-1 second after opponent contacts the mat

common_counters.counter: Wide base with hips back to prevent elevation
common_counters.your_response: Transition to leg entanglement attacks or Single Leg X when opponent refuses to engage forward

common_counters.counter: Back step to escape leg hooks before sweep initiates
common_counters.your_response: Follow with re-inversion and pursuit, or transition to Reverse De La Riva as they circle

common_counters.counter: Forward sprawl to flatten the inverted guard
common_counters.your_response: Use their forward pressure against them with rolling ankle lock entry or modified elevation

common_counters.counter: Grip fighting to strip ankle controls
common_counters.your_response: Release grips and attack with inside ashi entry while they focus on hands rather than leg positioning

common_errors.error: Insufficient hip elevation before attempting sweep
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily bases out and may pass to side control or flatten the guard completely
common_errors.correction: Focus on driving hips to maximum height before pulling on ankles - the elevation creates the leverage

common_errors.error: Shallow leg hooks that slip off during elevation
common_errors.consequence: Opponent's legs escape during sweep attempt, leaving you inverted with no control
common_errors.correction: Curl feet tightly around the back of opponent's thighs and maintain active tension throughout

common_errors.error: Rolling onto one shoulder during the sweep motion
common_errors.consequence: Destroys the platform needed for hip drive and typically results in failed sweep with poor position
common_errors.correction: Keep weight distributed across both shoulder blades and think of driving straight up rather than at an angle

common_errors.error: Releasing ankle grips too early during elevation
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can step backward to recover base and escape the sweep
common_errors.correction: Maintain pulling pressure on ankles throughout the entire sweep motion until you begin mounting

common_errors.error: Attempting sweep against opponent with wide base and hips back
common_errors.consequence: Sweep fails and exposes you to guard passing or disengagement
common_errors.correction: Recognize this defensive posture and transition to leg attacks or alternative sweeps instead

common_errors.error: Not following through to mount after successful elevation
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recovers guard or scrambles before you establish top position
common_errors.correction: Commit fully to the sweep - your body should follow opponent through the motion directly into mount

training_progressions.description: Practice establishing and holding the inverted grasshopper position with proper shoulder base and hip elevation. Work on maintaining the position for 20-30 second intervals without partner resistance.
With compliant partner, practice inserting leg hooks and establishing ankle grips. Focus on hook depth and maintaining connection as partner makes small movements. No sweep attempts yet.
Execute full sweep against partner giving 50% resistance. Partner provides forward pressure cues for timing. Focus on explosive hip drive and following through to mount position.
Incorporate sweep into live rolling from grasshopper guard. Work on recognizing sweep opportunities versus when to transition to leg attacks or other options. Full resistance with training partners.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Variation using only one leg hook while the other leg pushes on opponent's hip or chest for additional leverage. Useful when opponent defends one hook but leaves the other open.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent successfully strips one hook but maintains forward pressure

variants_and_adaptations.description: Instead of elevating directly up, add a rolling motion that carries opponent over your shoulder. Creates more momentum but requires more flexibility and timing.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against opponents with strong base who resist direct elevation

variants_and_adaptations.description: Executed without ankle grips, relying entirely on deep leg hooks and hip drive. Requires stronger core and more precise timing but leaves hands free for posting during transition.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: In no-gi when ankle grips are difficult to maintain

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the primary goal of Grasshopper Sweep?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary goal is to use hip elevation and leg hooks from the inverted Grasshopper Guard position to sweep the opponent directly to Mount, bypassing intermediate positions like Half Guard or Side Control entirely.

knowledge_assessment.question: What position do you start Grasshopper Sweep from?
knowledge_assessment.answer: This technique starts from Grasshopper Guard Bottom, an inverted open guard position where your shoulders rest on the mat with hips elevated and legs engaged with the opponent's lower body.

knowledge_assessment.question: What grips are most effective for controlling the Grasshopper Sweep?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The most effective grips are on the opponent's ankles, heels, or pants near the ankle area. These grips prevent the opponent from stepping back to recover base and provide additional pulling leverage during the hip elevation phase.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent widens their base and keeps their hips back when you establish Grasshopper Guard - how do you adjust?
knowledge_assessment.answer: When an opponent adopts this defensive posture, the Grasshopper Sweep becomes low percentage. Transition to leg entanglement attacks like Inside Ashi entry, or move to Single Leg X Guard where their wide base actually becomes a vulnerability rather than a strength.

knowledge_assessment.question: When is the optimal timing window to attempt the Grasshopper Sweep?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The optimal timing is when the opponent commits their weight forward, either by pressuring into the guard or attempting to establish grips on your legs. Their forward weight commitment provides the momentum needed for successful elevation and makes it difficult for them to base out backward.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most critical mechanical element that determines sweep success?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Maximum hip elevation before initiating the pulling motion is the most critical element. The hips must drive toward the ceiling first to create the upward force that lifts the opponent. Attempting to pull the opponent over without sufficient elevation results in failed sweeps and potential guard passes.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you adjust if your leg hooks start slipping during the sweep attempt?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If hooks begin slipping, immediately abort the sweep attempt and reset your leg position. Attempting to complete a sweep with compromised hooks typically fails and leaves you in a vulnerable inverted position. Reset by re-curling your feet deeply around the back of their thighs before attempting again.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the follow-up options if the Grasshopper Sweep is partially blocked but you maintain leg contact?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If the sweep is blocked but you maintain leg contact, immediately transition to leg attacks (kneebar entries or ankle lock attempts), recover to Single Leg X or X-Guard for alternative sweeps, or use the opponent's defensive reaction to re-invert and reset Grasshopper Guard for another attempt.

safety_considerations: The Grasshopper Sweep involves inverted positioning which places stress on the cervical spine and neck. Never attempt this technique with a stiff neck or existing cervical issues. During practice, partners should fall in a controlled manner rather than posting arms awkwardly which can cause wrist injuries. The rapid transition from inverted to mount creates momentum that must be controlled to avoid landing too heavily on training partners. Build inverted guard comfort gradually before attempting full speed sweeps. If you feel your neck taking weight during the technique, release and reset rather than forcing through the position.
position_integration: The Grasshopper Sweep integrates into the broader inverted guard and leg entanglement systems as a high-reward sweeping option. It functions best when paired with leg attack threats - opponents who fear the sweep must engage forward, opening leg entanglements, while those who defend leg attacks by staying back become vulnerable to the sweep. This creates a strategic dilemma typical of systematic approaches. The sweep commonly chains with Inside Ashi entries when blocked, X-Guard transitions when opponent bases wide, and Reverse De La Riva recovery when opponent back steps. Understanding when the sweep is available versus when to pivot to other attacks is essential for effective Grasshopper Guard play.
